You are implementing ONE requirement in the Apache Hadoop source tree at /workspace (a real upstream repo checked out at an earlier state).

REQUIREMENT SLUG: pmem-cache-persistence-docs
REQUIREMENT FILE: /workspace/requirements/pmem-cache-persistence-docs.yaml   <-- READ THIS FIRST

The `title:` field names the real upstream Apache Hadoop JIRA / git commit. Your job is to reproduce that upstream change as faithfully as you can from the requirement text plus the code you find in the tree. Hidden tests derived from the real upstream commit will grade the result, so EXACT naming matters:
  * new/changed configuration keys and their default values (and their entries in *-default.xml)
  * new class / interface / method / field / metric names and their visibility
  * log message wording and format placeholders
  * behavioural details (return values, exception types, ordering, off-by-one boundaries)
If the requirement text names an identifier (class, method, config key, metric, constant), use that identifier verbatim.

HOW TO WORK
1. Read the requirement yaml. Note the JIRA id and the module it belongs to (HDFS / YARN / MAPREDUCE / HADOOP-common / tools).
2. Locate the real code with Grep/Glob. Read enough surrounding code (and the existing tests for it) to make a correct, idiomatic change.
3. Implement the change. Match the surrounding code style, license headers, checkstyle habits (2-space indent, 80-col-ish, final where used, LOG placeholders `{}`).
4. If the change adds a config key, also add it to the matching `*-default.xml` (hdfs-default.xml / core-default.xml / yarn-default.xml / mapred-default.xml) with a sensible description, and to the `DFSConfigKeys`/`YarnConfiguration`/etc. constants class the module uses. Some modules have a TestYarnConfigurationFields / TestHdfsConfigFields style test that requires the xml and the constant to agree - keep them in sync.
5. If the upstream change would have come with tests, add or extend the corresponding test class under the same module (src/test/java/...). Keep tests deterministic and cheap. Do not add tests that need network or a real cluster beyond the usual MiniDFSCluster/MiniYARNCluster idioms already used in that test file.
6. Do NOT run maven/mvn or cmake (there is no warm build environment; it wastes your time). Instead be rigorous by inspection: every symbol you reference must exist (grep to confirm), every new import must be needed and correct, braces/parens balanced, no stale references left behind. Re-read your own final diff (`git diff -- <your files>`) before finishing and fix anything sloppy.
7. Scope discipline: change ONLY what this requirement needs. Do not reformat unrelated lines, do not fix unrelated warnings, do not touch other subsystems. Other agents are concurrently implementing ~380 other requirements in this same working tree.

FORBIDDEN COMMANDS (they would destroy other agents' concurrent work): git checkout / switch / stash / reset / revert / clean / rebase / merge / cherry-pick, `git add -A` or `git add .` without an explicit pathspec, `git commit --amend`, `git rm` of files you did not create, and any `mvn`/`gradle` invocation.

WHEN YOUR IMPLEMENTATION IS COMPLETE - commit it yourself with exactly this shape (substitute the real repo-relative paths you touched, space separated, and keep the flock):

  cd /workspace && flock /tmp/hadoop-git.lock bash -c 'git add -A -- PATH1 PATH2 ... && git diff --cached --binary > requirement_patches/pmem-cache-persistence-docs.diff && git commit -q -m "impl: pmem-cache-persistence-docs" && git log --oneline -1 && wc -c requirement_patches/pmem-cache-persistence-docs.diff'

Rules for that step:
  * List every file you created, modified or deleted as an explicit pathspec. Never a bare directory like `.`.
  * requirement_patches/pmem-cache-persistence-docs.diff MUST come out non-empty (wc -c > 0). If `git commit` reports "nothing to commit", another agent already committed your lines: verify the requirement is genuinely satisfied in the working tree, then report that in your notes.
  * Do not touch requirement_patches/ for any other slug.
  * IMPORTANT - a previous interrupted run left some UNCOMMITTED work in this tree. Before you start, run `cd /workspace && git status --short` and inspect `git diff` for the files you expect to touch. If part or all of this requirement is already implemented in the working tree but not yet committed, do NOT redo it from scratch: review it critically, finish/correct anything missing or wrong, then stage exactly those paths and commit as above. That uncommitted work is yours to claim when it belongs to this slug.

FINALLY return ONLY a JSON object (this is your return value, not a message to a human):
{"slug":"pmem-cache-persistence-docs","status":"done"|"partial"|"blocked","files":["..."],"committed":true|false,"patch_bytes":<int>,"summary":"<=3 sentences on what you changed","notes":"anything the orchestrator must know (conflicts, follow-ups, uncertainty)"}

title: HDFS-15788. Correct the statement for pmem cache to reflect cache persistence support
category: feature
requirement: '## Context

  Operators using SCM or PMEM caching need documentation that matches the actual persistence behavior, especially when deciding whether cached blocks should survive a DataNode restart.

  ## Desired outcome

  The documentation should clearly state that SCM cache persistence is supported and explain how `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery` changes restart behavior.

  ## Acceptance signals

  Operators can tell from the docs that enabling `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery=true` recovers persisted cache state on startup, while disabling it drops the previous SCM cache and requires recaching.

  '

input.command: git status --short | grep -i pmem; grep -rl "pmem.cache.recovery\|SCM cache\|CentralizedCacheManagement\|pmem" hadoop-hdfs-project/hadoop-hdfs/src/site/markdown/ -i 2>/dev/null

35:5.  HDFS supports non-volatile storage class memory (SCM, also known as persistent memory) cache in Linux platform. User can enable either memory cache or SCM cache for a DataNode. Memory cache and SCM cache can coexist among DataNodes. In the current implementation, the cache data in SCM will be cleaned up when DataNode restarts. Persistent HDFS cache support on SCM will be considered in the future.
51:The NameNode queries its set of *cache directives* to determine which paths should be cached. Cache directives are persistently stored in the fsimage and edit log, and can be added, removed, and modified via Java and command-line APIs. The NameNode also stores a set of *cache pools*, which are administrative entities used to group cache directives together for resource management and enforcing permissions.
205:Currently, there are two implementations for persistent memory cache. The default one is pure Java based implementation and the other is native implementation which leverages PMDK library to improve the performance of cache write and cache read.
209:1. Install PMDK library. Please refer to the official site http://pmem.io/ for detailed information.
219:Be sure to configure one of the following properties for DRAM cache or persistent memory cache. Please note that DRAM cache and persistent cache cannot coexist on a DataNode.
225:    This setting is shared with the [Lazy Persist Writes feature](./MemoryStorage.html). The Data Node will ensure that the combined memory used by Lazy Persist Writes and Centralized Cache Management does not exceed the amount configured in `dfs.datanode.max.locked.memory`.
227:*   dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.dirs
229:    This property specifies the cache volume of persistent memory. For multiple volumes, they should be separated by “,”, e.g. “/mnt/pmem0, /mnt/pmem1”. The default value is empty. If this property is configured, the volume capacity will be detected. And there is no need to configure `dfs.datanode.max.locked.memory`.
261:*   dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery
263:    This parameter is used to determine whether to recover the status for previous cache on persistent memory during the start of DataNode. If it is enabled, DataNode will recover the status for previously cached data on persistent memory. Thus, re-caching data will be avoided. If this property is not enabled, DataNode will clean up the previous cache, if any, on persistent memory. This property can only work when persistent memory is enabled, i.e., `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.dirs` is configured.

28	
29	2.  Because DataNode caches are managed by the NameNode, applications can query the set of cached block locations when making task placement decisions. Co-locating a task with a cached block replica improves read performance.
30	
31	3.  When block has been cached by a DataNode, clients can use a new , more-efficient, zero-copy read API. Since checksum verification of cached data is done once by the DataNode, clients can incur essentially zero overhead when using this new API.
32	
33	4.  Centralized caching can improve overall cluster memory utilization. When relying on the OS buffer cache at each DataNode, repeated reads of a block will result in all *n* replicas of the block being pulled into buffer cache. With centralized cache management, a user can explicitly pin only *m* of the *n* replicas, saving *n-m* memory.
34	
35	5.  HDFS supports non-volatile storage class memory (SCM, also known as persistent memory) cache in Linux platform. User can enable either memory cache or SCM cache for a DataNode. Memory cache and SCM cache can coexist among DataNodes. In the current implementation, the cache data in SCM will be cleaned up when DataNode restarts. Persistent HDFS cache support on SCM will be considered in the future.
36	
37	Use Cases
38	---------
39	
40	Centralized cache management is useful for files that accessed repeatedly. For example, a small *fact table* in Hive which is often used for joins is a good candidate for caching. On the other hand, caching the input of a *one year reporting query* is probably less useful, since the historical data might only be read once.
41	
42	Centralized cache management is also useful for mixed workloads with performance SLAs. Caching the working set of a high-priority workload insures that it does not contend for disk I/O with a low-priority workload.

Memory cache and SCM cache can coexist among DataNodes. Persistent HDFS cache support on SCM is supported by setting `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery` to true, which allows the DataNode to recover its previously cached data on persistent memory when it restarts, avoiding the need to re-cache. If this property is not enabled, the cache data in SCM will be cleaned up when DataNode restarts, and the blocks will need to be re-cached.
